lead: A count-based language model gives an n-gram probability zero if that n-gram never appeared in training. One zero kills a sentence probability, because sentence probability is a product of terms. Smoothing fixes this by moving a small amount of probability mass from seen n-grams to unseen ones. Interpolation and backoff combine a detailed high-order model with a safer low-order model. Classic n-gram systems in phone keyboards, speech recognition and statistical MT use some form of this.
prereq: You need: 2.1, especially the count matrix and the maximum likelihood estimate.

sections.h3: Why a zero count is fatal

blocks.text: In 2.1 the probability of a sentence w1…wm is the product of P(wi | context) over all words. If any factor is 0, the whole product is 0. A trigram model has many possible trigrams, and most never appear in a small corpus. A test sentence then gets probability 0. The log probability becomes −∞ and perplexity becomes infinite; see 2.3.

blocks.where: c(w) is the number of times word w occurs; N is the total number of word tokens. For a conditional n-gram, P<sub>MLE</sub>(w<sub>i</sub> | h) = c(h w<sub>i</sub>) / c(h), where h is the history, that is, the previous n−1 words.

blocks.text: Smoothing assigns nonzero probability to unseen events. It does not invent data. It reserves part of the total probability mass for events not seen in training. The same idea applies to unigrams and to n-grams with a history.

Add-one smoothing adds 1 to every count. For unigrams, P<sub>add1</sub>(w) = (c(w)+1)/(N+V). Here V is the number of word types in the vocabulary. The denominator is N+V, not N. For a conditional n-gram, P<sub>add1</sub>(w<sub>i</sub> | h) = (c(h w<sub>i</sub>)+1)/(c(h)+V). If c(h w<sub>i</sub>) is 0, the numerator is 1, so the probability is nonzero.

blocks.where: k is the smoothing amount, a small positive number. k=1 gives add-one. k<1 gives less mass to unseen words. k is chosen on held-out data. V is the vocabulary size, including words with count 0.

blocks.text: Discounting is a different route. Take a little probability from each seen count and give it to unseen events. Good-Turing gives one line of intuition: the total mass for unseen events is estimated from the number of n-grams seen exactly once, called singletons. Add-one is simple but gives too much mass to unseen words when V is large.

Linear interpolation mixes models of different orders with weights λ. A common trigram form is P(w<sub>i</sub> | h) = λ<sub>1</sub>P<sub>trigram</sub> + λ<sub>2</sub>P<sub>bigram</sub> + λ<sub>3</sub>P<sub>unigram</sub>, with λ<sub>1</sub>+λ<sub>2</sub>+λ<sub>3</sub>=1 and every λ≥0. If the trigram count is zero, its term is zero, but the bigram and unigram terms still give a nonzero result. The λ are not set on training data. Choose them on held-out data to maximise held-out likelihood or to minimise perplexity. A two-model form is P = λP<sub>bigram</sub> + (1−λ)P<sub>unigram</sub>.

Katz backoff works differently. If c(h w<sub>i</sub>) is greater than 0, use the discounted conditional count. If it is 0, back off to a shorter history. The form is P<sub>katz</sub>(w<sub>i</sub> | h) = c*(h w<sub>i</sub>)/c(h) when c(h w<sub>i</sub>)>0, and α(h)P<sub>katz</sub>(w<sub>i</sub> | h′) otherwise. Here h′ drops the oldest word from h, c* is the discounted count (c*<c for discounted counts; high counts may keep c*=c), and α(h) is a normalising factor that makes probabilities sum to 1 over all words. Backoff does not mix all orders at once; it uses the longer context only when that context was seen.

spec.title: Worked example: P(dog | the), N = 10, V = 6
spec.aria: A flow diagram of the worked example: the zero MLE bigram and the add-one unigram 1/16 for dog are multiplied by 0.7 and 0.3 and combined into P(dog | the) = 0.01875.

examples.question: A corpus has N = 10 word tokens. The unigram counts are the 4, cat 2, sat 2, on 1, mat 1, dog 0. The vocabulary has V = 6 words, because dog is a known word that never appeared. Find the maximum likelihood and add-one estimates for the and dog. Then find the interpolated bigram P(dog | the) using λ<sub>bigram</sub> = 0.7 and λ<sub>unigram</sub> = 0.3. The bigram count c(the dog) is 0. Use the maximum likelihood estimate for the bigram term and the add-one estimate for the unigram term.
steps: N = 10 tokens and V = 6 word types.
c(the dog) = 0, so the MLE bigram P<sub>bigram</sub>(dog | the) = 0.
Interpolated value using the MLE bigram and add-one unigram: 0.7×0 + 0.3×0.0625 = 0.01875.
examples.answer: The maximum likelihood estimates are 0.40 for the and 0 for dog; the add-one estimates are 0.3125 for the and 0.0625 for dog; using the MLE bigram and add-one unigram, the interpolated bigram probability P(dog | the) is 0.01875, about 0.019.
examples.check:
N = 10
V = 6
c_the = 4
c_dog = 0
lam_bigram = 0.7
lam_unigram = 0.3
p_mle_the = c_the / N
p_add1_the = (c_the + 1) / (N + V)
p_mle_dog = c_dog / N
p_add1_dog = (c_dog + 1) / (N + V)
p_bigram_dog_given_the = 0.0
p_interp = lam_bigram * p_bigram_dog_given_the + lam_unigram * p_add1_dog
print(p_mle_the)
print(p_add1_the)
print(p_mle_dog)
print(p_add1_dog)
print(p_interp)

traps: Using N instead of N+V in the add-one denominator. The probabilities then sum to more than 1.
Choosing λ values that do not sum to 1, or tuning λ on training data instead of held-out data.
Confusing interpolation with backoff. Interpolation mixes all orders; backoff switches to a shorter context only when the longer count is zero.
Reporting a maximum likelihood zero as a smoothed probability without saying which smoothing method was used.

quiz.q: In add-one smoothing, what does V mean?
quiz.a: V is the number of word types in the vocabulary, including words with count 0.

quiz.q: Why is a single zero probability fatal for a sentence probability?
quiz.a: Sentence probability is a product of word probabilities. One factor equal to 0 makes the whole product 0, so log probability is −∞ and perplexity is infinite.

quiz.q: N = 10 and V = 6. A word has count 0. Find its add-one probability.
P<sub>bigram</sub> = 0, P<sub>unigram</sub> = 0.1, λ<sub>bigram</sub> = 0.8 and λ<sub>unigram</sub> = 0.2. Find the interpolated probability.
Why are the interpolation weights λ chosen on held-out data?
quiz.a: Training data always likes weights that fit seen n-grams. Held-out data shows which weights give better probability to unseen text.

quiz.q: A trigram count is nonzero. Compare what interpolation and Katz backoff do with this trigram.
quiz.a: Interpolation still adds weighted bigram and unigram terms. Backoff uses the discounted trigram probability and does not switch to a shorter history.

quiz.q: Why does add-one smoothing give too much probability to unseen words when V is large?
quiz.a: Each of the V word types gets +1, so the total pseudo-count mass is V/(N+V). The z word types with count 0 get z/(N+V) in total, and each such type gets 1/(N+V). When V is large compared with N, this added mass is a large share, so unseen types as a group receive too much and seen words lose mass.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern neural language models replace explicit n-gram smoothing with subword tokenisation and softmax outputs, so unseen words rarely get exact zero. Kneser-Ney smoothing, an extension of backoff with continuation counts, is still a strong baseline for small corpora. Search terms: Laplace smoothing, Good-Turing, Katz backoff, Kneser-Ney, held-out likelihood.
